findings.title: SQL injection in the login query
findings.summary: The login route builds its SQL by inserting the submitted user name into the query text with an f-string, so a crafted name changes the query.

evidence.quote: row = DB.execute(f"SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = '{user}' AND pw = '{pw_hash}'").fetchone()

data_flow: app.py:17 reads the user name from request.form with no validation
app.py:19 inserts it into an f-string SQL statement
app.py:19 executes the statement with DB.execute
findings.attacker: Anyone who can reach /login. No account is needed.
findings.impact_detail: Authentication can be bypassed and the users table read, because the name is trusted as SQL.
findings.fix: Use a parameterised query: DB.execute('SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = ? AND pw = ?', (user, pw_hash)).
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Command injection in the export route
findings.summary: The export route appends the fmt query parameter to a shell command and runs it with shell=True.
data_flow: app.py:48 reads fmt from request.args with no allow-list
app.py:49 concatenates it into a command string
app.py:49 runs the string through a shell with shell=True
findings.attacker: Anyone who can reach /admin/export; see F-003, there is no authentication on the route.
findings.impact_detail: Arbitrary commands run as the web process.
findings.fix: Check fmt against an allow-list (csv, json), and pass an argument list without shell=True.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Admin export has no authentication or authorisation
findings.summary: Other routes check the session, but /admin/export checks nothing, so the admin function is open to anyone.
data_flow: app.py:46 registers the route
app.py:47 the handler goes straight to the export with no session or role check
findings.attacker: Anyone who can reach the application.
findings.impact_detail: An unauthenticated user can trigger the export, and with F-002 run commands.
findings.fix: Require a logged-in user with an admin role before the handler body runs, and deny by default.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Any logged-in user can read any booking
findings.summary: The booking route checks that someone is logged in, but not that the booking belongs to them, so changing the id returns other people's bookings.

evidence.quote: row = DB.execute("SELECT * FROM bookings WHERE id = ?", (booking_id,)).fetchone()

data_flow: app.py:27 takes booking_id from the URL
app.py:28 only checks that a session exists
app.py:30 selects the row by id with no owner condition
findings.impact_detail: Guest details for every booking can be enumerated by counting ids.
findings.fix: Add the owner to the query (AND user_id = ?) with session['uid'], and return 404 when no row matches.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Path traversal in the invoice download
findings.summary: The file parameter is joined to the invoices folder and sent back without checking where it resolves, so ../ sequences or an absolute path escape the folder.
data_flow: app.py:36 reads file from request.args
app.py:37 joins it to 'invoices' with os.path.join, which discards the folder if the value is an absolute path
app.py:37 sends whatever file results
findings.impact_detail: Arbitrary files readable by the web process can be downloaded, including the database and keys.
findings.fix: Use flask.send_from_directory('invoices', name), which rejects traversal, and allow only known file names.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Server-side request forgery in the preview route
findings.summary: The preview route fetches any URL supplied by the caller and returns the body, so the server can be made to request internal addresses.
data_flow: app.py:42 reads url from request.args
app.py:43 requests it with no scheme, host or address check
app.py:43 returns the response body to the caller
findings.impact_detail: Internal services and cloud metadata endpoints can be read through the server.
findings.fix: Allow-list hosts, resolve and block private and link-local ranges, disallow redirects, and return only what is needed.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Hard-coded session signing key
findings.summary: The Flask secret key is a literal in the source, so anyone with the repository can forge session cookies.
data_flow: app.py:11 sets the signing key to a constant string
app.py:21 and app.py:28 trust the session contents signed with it
findings.attacker: Anyone who can read the source, then send a forged cookie with any uid.
findings.impact_detail: Impersonation of any user, including administrators if roles are ever added.
findings.fix: Load the key from the environment or a secret store, generate a long random value, and rotate the key now that it is public.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.summary: Passwords are stored as plain MD5 digests, which are fast to brute force and identical for identical passwords.
data_flow: app.py:18 hashes the submitted password with MD5 and no salt
app.py:19 compares it with the stored value
findings.attacker: Anyone who obtains the users table, for example through F-001.
findings.impact_detail: Most passwords can be recovered quickly offline.
findings.fix: Use a slow password hash such as argon2id or bcrypt through a maintained library, and migrate existing hashes on next login.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Debug mode on and listening on all interfaces
findings.summary: The entry point starts the development server with debug=True on 0.0.0.0, which exposes the interactive debugger to the network.
data_flow: app.py:54 binds to every interface
app.py:54 enables debug mode, which serves an interactive debugger on errors
findings.attacker: Anyone on the network who can trigger an error page, if the server is started this way.
findings.impact_detail: Code execution through the debugger console.
findings.fix: Never run the development server in production: use a production server, bind to localhost behind a proxy, and set debug from configuration that defaults to off.
findings.verified_by: A second pass confirmed the line is reached when the module is run directly. Whether production runs it this way was not visible in the repository.

findings.title: Pull request workflow runs untrusted code with a secret
findings.summary: The workflow triggers on pull_request_target, checks out the pull request's own commit, runs its dependencies and tests, and passes a deploy token into that step.
data_flow: .github/workflows/ci.yml:3 runs with the base repository's secrets in the context of a pull request
.github/workflows/ci.yml:10 and .github/workflows/ci.yml:12 check out the attacker-controlled head commit
.github/workflows/ci.yml:13 installs and runs code from that commit
.github/workflows/ci.yml:15 exposes DEPLOY_TOKEN to that code
findings.attacker: Anyone who can open a pull request, including from a fork.
findings.impact_detail: The deploy token can be stolen by a test file or a dependency in the pull request.
findings.fix: Use the pull_request trigger for untrusted code, keep secrets out of that job, and if pull_request_target is needed, do not check out or run the head commit.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Support agent runs a model-chosen shell command built from ticket text
findings.summary: Ticket text, written by customers, is passed to the model, and whatever command the model returns is executed in a shell with no allow-list and no approval.

evidence.quote: plan = complete("You are a support agent. Decide a shell command to resolve this ticket:\n" + ticket_text)

data_flow: agent.py:8 puts untrusted ticket_text into the prompt
agent.py:8 takes the model's reply as a command
agent.py:9 runs it with shell=True and returns the output
findings.attacker: Anyone who can submit a support ticket, using prompt injection in the ticket text.
findings.impact_detail: Arbitrary commands run as the agent's process.
findings.fix: Do not execute model output. Offer a fixed set of typed actions with parameter validation, run them with least privilege, and require human approval for anything that changes state.
findings.verified_by: A second pass re-read the route from request to sink and found no validation, escaping or authorisation in between.

findings.title: Guest note is rendered as HTML
findings.summary: The page assigns guest_note to innerHTML, which would run any script in it. Whether an outsider can set guest_note could not be seen, because the code that writes it is not in this snapshot.
findings.to_validate: Find where guest_note is written (not in this repository snapshot). If guests or other low-privilege users can set it and staff view it, this becomes a confirmed stored XSS: test by saving a note with a harmless marker element and loading it as staff.

findings.title: Search box value inserted as HTML
findings.summary: The search handler writes the typed text into innerHTML.
findings.rejection_reason: The value comes from the user's own keystrokes in their own browser. There is no way for another person to set it through a link or stored data, so this is self-XSS with no attacker. Worth tidying with textContent, but not a vulnerability.
